sn22.22:1.2: This discourse is much-quoted in later texts of both Pali and Sanskrit Buddhism, especially in discussing what the Buddha meant by “person” (_puggala_). One school of Buddhism, the Pudgalavādins, argued that the “person” was as real as anything else, even if it could not be well defined, a position that was rejected by other schools, including the Theravada ([kv1.1]()). The text itself uses a subtle complex of imagery to make its point. Notably, the opening phrase clearly indicates three of the four noble truths (the burden is suffering, picking up is the origin, putting down is the cessation), leaving the status of the bearer of the burden unclear: is this a way of speaking about the path?
sn22.22:1.5: Vedic _skandha_ has no technical use, being simply the “trunk” of a tree (Rig Veda 1.32.5, Atharva Veda 10.7.38) or a person (plural = “shoulders”, Atharva Veda 6.25.2, 6.135.1, etc.). Chandogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1 mentions three people whose “trunks are religious duty” (_dharmaskandha_). As a technical term it shares more in common with the Jains, for whom the _skandha_ was a type of matter (_pudgala_) consisting of two or more combined “atoms” (_aṇu_), namely a “molecule” (Tattvārthasūtra 5.5). Thus the aggregates themselves can be considered what “shoulders” the burden (like buffaloes, Arthaśāstra 2.29.8).
sn22.22:2.1: This term is attested almost entirely in discussion of this discourse. However, we also find an unrelated idiomatic use in the commentary to [an3.91](), where it means “one who takes responsibility”.
sn22.22:2.2: _Puggala_ (Sanskrit _pudgala_) is a primarily Buddhist and Jain term, being absent from pre-Buddhist texts. Pali is rich in terms for a “person” (_purisa_, _jana_, _jantu_, _nara_, _manussa_), raising the question why _puggala_ is used. _Puggala_ is the normal term used especially in the Aṅguttara Nikāya when describing certain “individuals” and their characteristics; these are collected in the Abhidhamma book the Puggalapaññatti. The Jain meaning of _pudgala_ is “mass”, “matter” (Tattvārthasūtra 5.5). That this sense is not peculiar to the Jains is shown by its use for a “mass” (of gold) by Kauṭilya (Arthaśastra 2.14.7, 2.14.43). In this way the word _puggala_ connects with the idea of _khandha_ as an “aggregate”, “bundle”. Perhaps the Buddha favored this term because it avoided Vedic terminology, while at the same time suggesting a connection with the _khandha_ doctrine that the “person” comprised a “mass” of components. Indeed, related to a criticism of those who believe in not-self, i.e. Buddhists, we find _pudgalāśrayāḥ_ (“comprised of a composite mass”, Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.30.13). Try reading this Sutta and substituting “mass” for “person”.
sn22.22:2.3: It is curious that the “person” is referred to as “venerable”. Perhaps this is meant to imply that they have “undertaken responsibility” for the path of practice, thus standing in for the otherwise-missing fourth noble truth.
